correctness.rationale: For each fixed induced H subset, conditioning on the induced isomorphism class leaves external edges independent, and an overlapping r-set clique has precisely c_s(H) favorable s-subsets. The resulting exact normalized covariance is a positive-coefficient sum of decreasing powers of p minus constants. When 0<e(H)<C(m,2), the s=2 derivative is strictly negative, the p->0 limit positive infinite, and the p->1 limit negative, proving a unique interior zero. Empty and complete patterns have strict uniform signs. The first-order critical point is derived by taking the ratio of binomial coefficients at overlaps 3 and 2, with higher overlaps O((n-m)^-2). Direct exact enumeration passes 168 finite comparisons; these checks are corroboration, not infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The proposed contribution is the all-induced-motif/all-clique-size single covariance sign-switch classification and the critical-location triangle-excess law. Relevant full-text graph-factor and subgraph-deviation results were inspected, and a known three-vertex wedge/triangle special case was compared; neither supplies the general global sign theorem as a stated result. The generic graph-factor method offers a plausible route to related identities, so conclusive historical priority remains open.
residual_risks: The original Janson 1994 and Janson 1995 graph Fourier treatments were not read in full; an equivalent general statement or easy implication may be there.
Ellis–Ferry 2010 was not read in full; it concerns general overlapping subgraphs but may indirectly encode the specific calculation.

A general published graph-factor coefficient identity can facilitate a derivation of the exact covariance. The claimed genuinely new component is a universal sign classification; its publication priority needs human literature review.

value.rationale: The result gives a natural complete classification for every induced network pattern and every clique order in a basic random graph model, replacing complex motif-by-motif sign calculations with exactly one transition; the sharp first correction singles out triangle excess, and two equal-edge-density 5-vertex motifs have opposite correlations with both triangles and 4-cliques. These are structural, interpretable consequences rather than arbitrary finite computations. The finite sign law is useful for jointly interpreting graphlet and clique statistics, without claiming an unproved estimator or generalization.
